title: DC's Supergirl Opened in India. Bollywood Didn't Even Blink.
excerpt: Milly Alcock brought Kara Zor-El to Indian cinemas with Jason Momoa and a James Gunn seal of approval. She left with ₹4 crore and a hard lesson about who owns this box office now.
body:
The new DC Universe had one job: make people care about superheroes again. In America, Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow managed a decent if unspectacular opening. In India? It opened to near-silence — and the silence was deafening.

Milly Alcock, who was absolute fire as young Rhaenyra Targaryen in House of the Dragon, steps into the suit as Kara Zor-El in Craig Gillespie's interstellar revenge odyssey. She's angry, she's powerful, and she's carrying the weight of DC's entire post-reboot credibility on her cape. The film also features Matthias Schoenaerts, Eve Ridley as the scene-stealing Ruthye, Jason Momoa, and David Corenswet — yes, the new Superman shows up, connecting Supergirl directly to next year's Superman: Man of Tomorrow.

On paper, this should work in India. Superhero films have historically had a floor here. Hindi, Tamil, and Telugu dubs were ready. The DC brand still carries weight. And Alcock has a fanbase in India thanks to House of the Dragon's massive streaming numbers on JioHotstar.

The numbers, however, are brutal.

Supergirl opened to approximately ₹1.40 crore on Day 1 in India. It stayed flat on Day 2. By the end of its first weekend, the total stood at just ₹3.94 crore across nearly 2,400 screens — an overall occupancy of barely 11%. The kind of opening that makes a mid-budget Hindi film nervous and makes a Hollywood tentpole look actively invisible.

What happened? Two words: Welcome To The Jungle.

Akshay Kumar's comedy behemoth landed on the exact same date — June 26 — and simply ate every available screen, showtime, and ticket budget in the country. While Welcome To The Jungle was pulling ₹14.80 crore on Day 1 and crashing past ₹60 crore by Sunday, Supergirl was playing to half-empty multiplexes in Mumbai, Delhi, and Bengaluru. By Monday, the conversation wasn't about whether Kara could recover — it was about whether theatres would even keep her shows running through the week.

The clash was brutal, but blaming it entirely on Akshay Kumar misses the bigger picture. Indian audiences aren't reflexively showing up for every cape anymore. The MCU's grip has loosened since Endgame, and the DC brand has been in perpetual reboot mode for so long that audiences have genuinely lost track of which universe they're even in. Aquaman 2 underperformed here. The Flash barely registered. By the time James Gunn's carefully rebooted DCU launched its first film, the Indian market had already moved on to a different kind of spectacle — one that speaks their language, literally.

And that's the real story. While Supergirl struggled to cross ₹4 crore, Cocktail 2 was cruising past ₹127 crore worldwide. Alpha's teaser was generating 75 million views in 24 hours. Ramayana was dominating conversations at Comic-Con. Indian cinema isn't just competing with Hollywood anymore — it's making Hollywood feel like the import nobody asked for.

"Audiences are more than willing to show up in droves, provided the promise is that of a larger-than-life experience they can't get on their living room screens." — Sacnilk's 2026 Box Office Analysis

For the diaspora, though, this is a different equation. If you're in the US, UK, or Canada, Supergirl is actually worth your time. Alcock brings a rawness to Kara that's genuinely compelling — this isn't a bright-eyed hero learning to fly. This is a grieving, furious woman on a vengeance quest across alien worlds, and the film's lean 109-minute runtime keeps it punchy. Craig Gillespie — the man behind I, Tonya and Cruella — knows how to direct complicated women, and it shows.

Eve Ridley's Ruthye — a young alien whose father is murdered, setting the whole plot in motion — is the emotional heart of the film. Her narration gives it a fairy-tale quality that's unusual for superhero fare. And Jason Momoa's appearance, while brief, hints at the interconnected DC Universe that Gunn is patiently assembling.

The film feels streaming-adjacent in pacing and tone — which may explain why Indian theatrical audiences didn't bite. This is one that'll find its real audience on OTT when it inevitably drops on Max or JioCinema in a few months. Diaspora viewers with streaming subscriptions, bookmark it.

But in Indian cinemas, the verdict is clear: Kara Zor-El couldn't outfly Akshay Kumar in a jungle. In 2026, that tells you everything about where the power really lies.
